title: Finding files with find
about: How find walks a tree and evaluates tests and actions: names, types, sizes, times, permissions, operators and precedence, exec, delete, xargs, and the classic traps.

questions.title: What find searches
questions.text: What does `find` look at when it searches?

options.t: The attributes of files and directories (name, type, size, owner, time, permissions), walking a directory tree recursively.
options.why: It does not read file contents; that is `grep`'s job.

options.t: Only the current directory, without sub-directories.
options.why: It recurses by default (unless `-maxdepth` is used).

options.t: A database of file names updated daily.
options.why: That is `locate`; `find` walks the real file system each time.

questions.title: Default starting point
questions.text: Which statement about `find` without arguments is true (with GNU find)?

options.t: It starts from the current directory and prints everything below it.
It searches the whole file system from `/`.
It prints an error about the missing path.
It prints only the hidden files.

questions.title: Anatomy of a find command
questions.text: Match each part of `find /etc -name '*.conf' -print` with its role.

pairs.r: A test that keeps only matching names
An action that writes the path
pairs.why: The default action when none is given.

pairs.r: A glob pattern that find itself interprets
pairs.why: Quoted so the shell leaves it alone.

extras.why: None of the words is a redirection.

questions.title: Quote the pattern
questions.text: Why is `find . -name "*.txt"` written with quotes?

options.t: So that the shell does not expand `*.txt` into file names of the current directory before `find` runs.

options.why: It is the shell's expansion that causes trouble.

questions.title: The unquoted pattern trap
questions.text: In a directory that contains the single file `one.txt`, you run `find . -name *.txt`. What happens?

options.t: The shell turns `*.txt` into `one.txt`, so `find` looks for files named exactly `one.txt` everywhere, and misses all other `.txt` files.
options.why: The command silently finds less than you wanted.

options.t: `find` lists every `.txt` file of the tree.

options.why: It runs normally with the wrong pattern.

options.t: `find` lists only `one.txt` in the current directory.
options.why: It searches the whole tree for that name.

questions.title: Case-insensitive name search
questions.text: To match `.txt`, `.TXT` and `.Txt`: `find . {{0}} '*.txt'`

questions.title: -name and paths
questions.text: Why does `find . -name 'a/x.txt'` never find anything?

options.t: `-name` compares the pattern only against the last component (the base name) of each path; use `-path` for patterns that contain slashes.

options.why: The behaviour is independent of that.

options.t: Because `-name` only works in the current directory.
options.why: It works on the whole tree.

questions.title: Patterns find understands
questions.text: Select the true statements about the pattern of `-name`.

options.t: It uses glob syntax (`*`, `?`, `[...]`), not regular expressions.
It is matched against the file name only, not the directory part.
A leading dot is matched by `*` (unlike in shell globbing), so hidden files are found.
It is a regular expression, so `.*\.txt` is the right form.

questions.title: Find tests and actions
questions.text: Classify each find primary.

items.why: Writes the path to standard output.
Runs a command for the file.

questions.title: -type letters
questions.text: Match each `-type` letter with the kind of file.

extras.why: Hidden files are found by name, not by type.

questions.title: Hidden files
questions.text: How do you find the files whose names start with a dot, directly in the current directory?

options.why: The pattern `.*` matches names that begin with a dot.
That matches names ending in a dot.

questions.title: Depth options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Only the starting directory and its direct children
Down to grandchildren of the start
Process each directory's contents before the directory itself
pairs.why: Needed for bottom-up work such as deleting.

questions.title: Only direct children
questions.text: Which command lists only the regular files directly inside `dir` (not in sub-directories)?

questions.title: Directories are files too
questions.text: Why does `find a -size +2k` also print directory names such as `a` or `a/b`?

options.t: Directories are files with their own size (often 4096 bytes), so a test on size matches them; add `-type f` to restrict to regular files.
options.why: Always combine size tests with `-type f` when you mean files.

options.t: Because `-size` counts the files *inside* the directory.
options.why: It uses the size of the directory entry itself.

options.t: Because `-size` ignores the type of file.
options.why: It does look at the size, but directories have one too.

questions.title: Whole path tests
questions.text: Which test matches the full path and is the right one for `*/src/*.c`?

options.why: Compares the pattern against the whole path.
That option selects a regex dialect.

questions.title: Size suffixes
questions.text: What does `find . -size +1M` select?

options.t: Files that use more than 1 mebibyte (rounded up to whole MiB).
Files that are at most 1 MB.
Files modified more than a minute ago.

questions.title: Size units
questions.text: Match each suffix of `-size` with its unit.

pairs.why: The historical default, often a surprise.

questions.title: Sizes are rounded up
questions.text: What does `find . -type f -size -1k` match?

options.t: Only empty files (size 0), because sizes are rounded up to whole units and "less than 1" therefore means zero units.

questions.title: Sizes exactly
questions.text: Which command finds files of exactly 100 bytes?

options.why: The `c` suffix counts bytes without rounding.

questions.title: Files over two megabytes
questions.text: Find the files under `/usr/lib` larger than 2 MiB: `find /usr/lib -type f -size {{0}}`
questions.note: A plus means "more than", a minus "less than", no sign "exactly".

wrong.why: Only files whose size rounds to exactly 2 MiB.

questions.title: Days and mtime
questions.text: A file was modified 36 hours ago. Which test matches it?

options.why: Ages are counted in whole 24-hour periods with the fraction dropped: 36 hours is 1 day.
That needs at least 2 full days.
It is not yet two days old.
That means less than one full day.

questions.title: Time tests
questions.text: Match each test with the files it selects.

pairs.r: Modified more than 7 full days ago
Modified less than one day ago
Modified more recently than the file `ref`
Last read more than 30 days ago

extras.why: `find` has no creation-time test in this form.

questions.title: Which time
questions.text: What does `-mtime` look at compared with `-ctime`?

options.t: `-mtime` is the last change of the file's contents; `-ctime` is the last change of its inode (permissions, owner, links, or contents).

options.why: Linux does not keep creation time in that field.

options.t: `-mtime` is the last time it was read.

questions.title: Recently modified
questions.text: List regular files changed in the last hour: `find . -type f {{0}} -60`

wrong.why: That counts days, so `-mtime -60` means less than 60 days.
That compares against a reference file.

questions.title: Permission tests
questions.text: Match each test with its meaning.

pairs.why: No more and no fewer bits.

pairs.r: All of the bits of 644 are set (others may be set too)
Any of the write bits is set

questions.title: Executable files
questions.text: Which command finds regular files that are executable by their owner?

options.why: At least the owner's execute bit is set.
Without a minus, find looks for exactly that mode.
That adds a condition about the owner.

questions.title: Writable by anyone
questions.text: Find files that are writable by **any** of owner, group or others: `find . -type f -perm {{0}}`
questions.note: `/mode` means "any of these bits"; `-mode` means "all of these bits".

wrong.why: That requires all three write bits at once.
Exactly mode 222, which is very rare.

questions.title: Owners and groups
questions.text: Select the tests that select files by owner or group.

options.why: Not a GNU find test (`-user` is).

questions.title: Empty files and directories
questions.text: Which option selects empty files and empty directories?

options.why: A zero-length file, or a directory without entries.
Finds zero-size files and, in practice, not empty directories (their size is not 0).

questions.title: Implicit and
questions.text: What does `find . -name '*.c' -type f` mean when no operator is given between the tests?

options.t: Both tests must be true (an implicit `-a`).
options.why: A file name ending in `.c` and a regular file.

options.t: The tests are evaluated in random order.
options.why: They are evaluated left to right.

questions.title: Or needs parentheses
questions.text: You want `.txt` or `.log` **regular files**. Which command is correct?

options.why: The escaped parentheses group the alternatives so that `-type f` applies to both.
The `-o` splits the expression: `-type f -name '*.txt'` or `-name '*.log'`; directories named `*.log` would match.
Unescaped parentheses belong to the shell and cause a syntax error.

questions.title: Precedence surprise
questions.text: What does `find a -name '*.txt' -o -name '*.log' -print` print?

options.t: Only the `.log` files: `-print` belongs to the right-hand side, because `-a` binds tighter than `-o`.
options.why: A `.txt` match is true but has no action, so nothing is printed for it.
That needs parentheses or no explicit `-print`.

questions.title: Default print
questions.text: Why does `find a -name '*.txt' -o -name '*.log'` (no explicit action) print both kinds?

options.t: When no action is given, `find` adds an implicit `-print` for the **whole** expression.
options.why: The trap appears only when you write one `-print` yourself.

options.t: Because `-o` combines the lists of results.
Because the default is to print only `.log` files.

questions.title: Negation
questions.text: Find every regular file whose name does **not** end in `.txt`: `find . -type f {{0}} -name '*.txt'`
questions.note: Use `\!` if your shell treats `!` specially (for example history expansion in an interactive session).

questions.title: Which files does this select
questions.text: Expression: `find . -type f \( -name '*.sh' -o -name '*.bin' \) -perm -u+x`. Decide for each file.

items.why: A `.bin` file the owner can execute.
Right name, but no execute bit.
Executable, but the name is neither `.sh` nor `.bin`.
The name fits, but it is not a regular file.
`-name` is case-sensitive, so `.BIN` does not match `*.bin`.

questions.title: exec semantics
questions.text: What does `find . -name '*.log' -exec rm {} \;` do?

options.t: It runs `rm` once per file found, replacing `{}` by the file name.
options.why: The `\;` ends the command given to `-exec`.

options.t: It removes every file of the directory.
It prints the names without deleting.
It runs `rm` once with all names.

questions.title: Semicolon versus plus
questions.text: What is the difference between `-exec cmd {} \;` and `-exec cmd {} +`?

options.t: With `;` the command runs once per file; with `+` many file names are appended to one command line, which is faster.
`+` runs the command on directories only.

questions.title: Escaping the semicolon
questions.text: Why must the semicolon after `-exec` be written as `\;` or `';'`?

options.t: An unescaped `;` would be interpreted by the shell as the end of the `find` command.

options.why: It accepts the plain character when it arrives.

options.t: Because `;` is not allowed in file names.

questions.title: Ask before
questions.text: Which action asks for confirmation before running the command for each file?

questions.title: The -delete trap
questions.text: Why is `find /tmp/work -name '*' -delete` dangerous?

options.t: It matches everything, including `/tmp/work` itself, so the directory and all it contains are removed.

options.why: It removes whatever matches (directories must be empty, which works because it deletes depth-first).

questions.title: Order of delete
questions.text: In `find q -name '*.tmp' -delete -print`, what do you see for a file `q/a.tmp`?

options.t: The path `q/a.tmp` is printed after it was deleted.
options.why: Actions run left to right; `-delete` succeeds, so `-print` follows.

options.t: Nothing is printed, `-delete` ends the expression.
`-print` runs first, then the file disappears.
An error, because two actions cannot be combined.

questions.title: Safe clean-up
questions.text: Put these steps in order to delete old log files safely.

items.t: Run `find /var/tmp -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -type f` to see the candidates
items.why: Only `-print` (the default) shows what would be deleted.

items.t: Check the list: expected names, nothing unexpected
Re-run the same command with `-delete` at the end
items.why: The action comes after all the tests.

items.t: Run the first command again to confirm nothing is left

questions.title: find and xargs
questions.text: Which command safely removes `.tmp` files whose names may contain spaces?

options.why: Null-separated names survive spaces and newlines.
Names with spaces split into several arguments.
Word splitting breaks names with spaces.

questions.title: Command substitution vs exec
questions.text: What is a disadvantage of `rm $(find . -name '*.bak')` compared with `find . -name '*.bak' -delete`?

options.t: The shell splits the result on whitespace (and may hit the argument-length limit), so unusual names are mishandled.
options.why: `find` does the job internally without such limits.

options.t: It is always slower for small directories.
It deletes only the first file.

questions.title: printf
questions.text: What does `find . -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf '%f %s\n'` print?

options.t: For each regular file: its base name and its size in bytes.
The full path and the owner.

questions.title: Skipping a directory
questions.text: Which expression lists the files of the current tree but does not descend into `./node_modules`?

options.why: `-prune` stops the descent; the `-o` makes the rest apply to other paths.
That excludes a file with that *name*, but still walks into the directory.
That does not look deeper at all.

questions.title: Big files
questions.text: Which command lists the regular files in `/var` larger than 100 MiB?

options.why: That is in 512-byte blocks, and includes directories.
Lists the usage of every directory, not individual files.

questions.title: Recently changed scripts
questions.text: Which command lists the shell scripts in your home directory modified in the last 7 days?

questions.title: Own writable files
questions.text: Which command lists the files of your home directory that you have permission to write?

options.why: `-writable` tests real write access of the current user.

questions.title: Copy found files
questions.text: Which command copies every `.sh` file found below the current directory into `~/backup`?

options.why: `cp` does not read file names from its standard input.
That passes `find` as a file name.
Redirects the list of names into a path that is a directory.

questions.title: Count matches
questions.text: Which command prints how many `.conf` files there are below `/etc`?

options.why: Counts lines in the files of one directory, not the files themselves.
`/etc` is a directory, and it would look inside the files.

questions.title: Contents or names
questions.text: Which command lists the files under `/etc` whose **contents** include the word `nameserver`?

questions.title: find versus locate
questions.text: Why can `locate` miss a file that `find` would find?

options.t: `locate` reads a prebuilt database that is refreshed periodically, so very recent files are not in it.
options.why: `find` looks at the real file system each time.
It searches the database of the whole system.
